claims.text: An ML-driven framework correlating composition, thermomechanical processing, and quantitative microstructure will enable discovery of HEAs with simultaneously improved strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
Traditional trial-and-error development of HEAs often produces modest or mutually exclusive improvements in mechanical properties.
Experimental HEA datasets can encode relationships among chemistry, processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties.
The training dataset will combine real-time SEM/EBSD or in situ diffraction characterization with mechanical-testing outcomes.
The trained model will predict optimized alloy compositions and thermomechanical-treatment protocols.
A sufficiently comprehensive, representative, and high-quality dataset is required for the methodology to work.
Mechanical testing should cover temperatures and strain rates typical of structural applications.
ML-guided design will produce a favorable microstructure with refined grains, tailored phase fractions, and enhanced local chemical order.
ML can identify correlations between processing, microstructure, and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Grain refinement and controlled precipitate distributions will strengthen the alloys while preserving or enhancing ductility and fracture resistance.
The unified ML strategy overcomes limitations of optimizing composition, processing, or properties in isolation.
ML-guided alloys will simultaneously improve yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture toughness by approximately 10–20% relative to state-of-the-art conventionally developed HEAs.
Some computationally designed HEAs can achieve greater stiffness while retaining low predicted ductility, illustrating a property trade-off.
Sparse training data can prevent the predicted improvements from being realized.
Environmental degradation, scale-up effects, or other uncontrolled experimental variability can prevent the predicted improvements.
Preliminary data-driven studies support the predicted direction of mechanical-property improvement.
The magnitude of improvement will vary with alloy system and processing conditions.
The proposed comparison will use ML-guided samples and conventionally developed control samples under identical testing conditions.
Failure to improve at least three of four measured properties by approximately 10% relative to the control will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires simultaneous 10–20% improvement in all four properties, whereas the falsification rule treats improvement in only three of four properties as sufficient to avoid falsification.

The intervention includes ML optimization of thermomechanical-treatment protocols, but the experiment states that ML-guided and control samples undergo identical thermomechanical processing, preventing a direct test of the optimized-processing component.
